title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World

topics.title: The human eye and defects of vision

learn.hook: Your eye is a camera that refocuses itself in a split second — from your phone screen to a kite high in the sky!
points: Light enters through the cornea, where most of the refraction happens. The iris controls the size of the pupil, which regulates how much light enters. The eye lens fine-tunes the focus to form a real, inverted image on the retina; the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

Power of accommodation: ciliary muscles change the eye lens's focal length. Relaxed muscles make the lens thinner (longer focal length) for distant objects; contracted muscles make it thicker (shorter focal length) for near objects. For a young adult with normal vision, the near point is about 25 cm and the far point is at infinity.

Myopia (near-sightedness): distant objects look blurred because the image forms in front of the retina; caused by excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball. Corrected with a concave lens.

Hypermetropia (far-sightedness): near objects look blurred because the image would form behind the retina; the near point is farther than 25 cm. Caused by too long a focal length of the eye lens or the eyeball being too small. Corrected with a convex lens.

Presbyopia: with age the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible, so the near point recedes; corrected with convex lenses, or bifocals (concave upper part for distance, convex lower part for reading) if both defects exist. In cataract, the lens becomes milky and cloudy; surgery can restore vision.

example.q: A student cannot see objects clearly beyond 2 m. What kind and power of lens does she need?
steps: She has myopia: her far point is 2 m instead of infinity.
A concave lens must make distant objects appear to come from 2 m, so f = −2 m.
example.answer: A concave lens of power −0.5 D

learn.reallife: Eye doctors advise taking breaks from screens and looking at distant objects now and then; if myopia does develop, spectacles with concave lenses correct it.

quiz.q: What is the near point of a young adult with normal vision?
quiz.explain: The least distance of distinct vision for a normal young eye is about 25 cm.
steps: The near point is the least distance at which we see clearly without strain.
For a young adult with normal vision it is about 25 cm.
The far point is at infinity.
So the near point is 25 cm.
Answer: 25 cm
quiz.mistake: Confuses the near point with the far point

quiz.q: Which part of the eye does most of the refraction of light?
quiz.explain: Most refraction happens at the outer surface of the cornea; the lens only fine-tunes the focus.
steps: Light first enters through the cornea.
Most of the refraction happens at the outer surface of the cornea.
The eye lens only fine-tunes the focus.
So the cornea does most of the refraction.
Answer: Cornea
quiz.mistake: Thinks the eye lens does all the bending

quiz.q: When we look at a distant tree, the ciliary muscles —
quiz.explain: Relaxed ciliary muscles let the lens become thin, increasing its focal length for distant objects.
steps: For a distant object the eye needs a longer focal length.
The ciliary muscles relax, so the lens becomes thinner.
So the ciliary muscles relax, making the lens thinner.
Answer: Relax, making the lens thinner
quiz.mistake: Reverses the action for near and far objects

quiz.q: A person cannot see distant objects clearly. Which lens corrects this defect?
quiz.explain: This is myopia; a concave (diverging) lens moves the image back onto the retina.
steps: Not seeing distant objects clearly is myopia.
The image forms in front of the retina.
A concave (diverging) lens moves the image back onto the retina.
So the correcting lens is a concave lens.
Answer: Concave lens
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the lenses for myopia and hypermetropia

quiz.q: A myopic person's far point is 2 m. What is the power of the correcting lens, in dioptres?
quiz.explain: f = −2 m (concave), so P = 1/f = −0.5 D.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign or uses P = f
steps: Required lens: concave, f = −2 m
Answer: -0.5

quiz.q: Which is a cause of hypermetropia?
options: The eyeball has become too small
Excessive curvature of the eye lens
Too much light entering the eye
quiz.explain: A short eyeball (or a lens with too long a focal length) makes light focus behind the retina.
steps: In hypermetropia light would focus behind the retina.
Causes: the eyeball is too small, or the eye lens has too long a focal length.
Elongated eyeball and excess curvature cause myopia.
So the cause here is that the eyeball has become too small.
Answer: The eyeball has become too small
quiz.mistake: Gives a cause of myopia instead

quiz.q: Why do many elderly people need reading glasses?
options: Presbyopia: ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible
quiz.explain: With age the power of accommodation decreases, so the near point moves farther away.
steps: With age the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible.
This is presbyopia: the near point moves farther away.
So elderly people need reading glasses (convex lenses).
Answer: Presbyopia: ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible
quiz.mistake: Confuses presbyopia with cataract

quiz.q: What happens in cataract?
options: The crystalline lens becomes milky and cloudy
quiz.explain: A cloudy lens blocks light, causing partial or total loss of vision; surgery can restore sight.
steps: In cataract the crystalline eye lens becomes milky and cloudy.
Light is blocked, causing partial or total loss of vision.
Surgery can restore sight.
Answer: The crystalline lens becomes milky and cloudy
quiz.mistake: Confuses cataract with myopia

teach.ask: Gappu squints at the blackboard: 'I can read my book but the board is blurry! What's wrong and how do glasses fix it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! That's myopia — the image forms in front of the retina, and a concave lens moves it back!
teach.nudge: Good! Which type of lens — convex or concave — corrects this defect?

revise.summary: The eye focuses light mainly at the cornea, with the lens adjusting focus by accommodation, to form a real, inverted image on the retina. Myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia are corrected with concave, convex and bifocal lenses; cataract makes the lens cloudy.

Explain accommodation for near and distant objects
Give the cause and correction of myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia
remember: Near point of a normal young eye ≈ 25 cm; far point = infinity
Distant objects: ciliary muscles relax, lens thinner; near objects: muscles contract, lens thicker
Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens; presbyopia → convex or bifocal lens
traps: Most refraction is at the cornea, not the eye lens
Don't swap the corrections: myopia needs a concave lens, not convex
An elongated eyeball causes myopia; a small eyeball causes hypermetropia

topics.title: Refraction through a prism and dispersion

learn.hook: Shine sunlight through a glass prism and out pops a rainbow — white light was hiding seven colours all along!
points: A triangular glass prism has two inclined refracting faces; the angle between them is the angle of the prism. Light bends towards the base, and the angle between the incident and emergent rays is the angle of deviation.
Dispersion: white light splits into its component colours — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red (VIBGYOR). This band of colours is a spectrum.
Different colours bend by different amounts: red bends the least and violet the most.

Isaac Newton first used a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. A second, identical prism placed upside down recombines the colours into white light, showing sunlight is made of seven colours.

A rainbow forms when tiny water droplets in the air after a shower act like small prisms: they refract and disperse sunlight, reflect it internally and refract it again. It is always seen opposite to the Sun.

example.q: Think it through: you want to see a rainbow on a sunny morning while watering plants with a hose. Which way should you face?
steps: A rainbow is formed by sunlight dispersed by water droplets.
The light is reflected back from inside the droplets towards the observer.
So the Sun must be behind you.
example.answer: Face away from the Sun (the Sun behind you), towards the water spray.

learn.reallife: The glittering colours from the cut-glass pieces of a chandelier at a Diwali party are small displays of light splitting into colours, just like in a prism.

games.title: Prism and rainbow facts
items: Red light bends the least in a prism.
Red is deviated least, violet most.
A prism adds colours to white light.
The colours are already in white light; the prism only separates them.
A second inverted prism can recombine the spectrum into white light.
Newton showed this, proving sunlight is a mixture of colours.
A rainbow is seen on the same side of the sky as the Sun.
A rainbow is always seen opposite to the Sun.
Water droplets act like tiny prisms in forming a rainbow.
They refract, disperse and internally reflect sunlight.
In a prism, light bends towards its base.
Both refractions bend the ray towards the base of the prism.

quiz.q: What is the splitting of white light into its component colours called?
quiz.explain: Dispersion happens because different colours bend by different amounts.
steps: White light passing through a prism splits into colours (VIBGYOR).
This splitting is called dispersion.
Scattering and reflection are different processes.
So the answer is dispersion.
Answer: Dispersion
quiz.mistake: Confuses dispersion with scattering

quiz.q: Which colour of light bends the most when passing through a prism?
quiz.explain: Violet is deviated most and red least.
steps: Different colours bend by different amounts in a prism.
Red bends the least and violet bends the most.
So violet light bends the most.
Answer: Violet
quiz.mistake: Reverses red and violet

quiz.q: Why does a prism split white light into colours?
options: Each colour bends through a different angle
Light reflects inside the prism many times
quiz.explain: The refractive index of glass is slightly different for each colour, so each is deviated by a different amount.
steps: The refractive index of glass is slightly different for each colour.
So each colour is deviated through a different angle.
That separates white light into its colours.
Answer: Each colour bends through a different angle
quiz.mistake: Thinks the prism has colours in it

quiz.q: Who first used a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight?
quiz.explain: Isaac Newton obtained the spectrum and recombined it with a second inverted prism.
steps: Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and obtained its spectrum.
He then recombined the colours with a second, inverted prism.
So the answer is Isaac Newton.
Answer: Isaac Newton
quiz.mistake: Links any light experiment with Raman

quiz.q: Which processes in water droplets form a rainbow?
options: Refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, then refraction again
quiz.explain: Sunlight is refracted and dispersed entering a droplet, reflected inside, and refracted again as it leaves.
steps: Sunlight is refracted and dispersed as it enters a droplet.
It is reflected inside the droplet (internal reflection).
It is refracted again as it leaves.
So: refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, then refraction again.
Answer: Refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, then refraction again
quiz.mistake: Thinks reflection alone gives colours

quiz.q: The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray in a prism is called the —
quiz.explain: It measures how much the prism has turned the ray from its original path.
steps: The prism turns the ray from its original path.
The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray measures this turn.
It is called the angle of deviation.
Answer: Angle of deviation
quiz.mistake: Confuses angle of deviation with angle of prism

quiz.q: In which direction must you look to see a rainbow?
options: Away from the Sun, with the Sun behind you
quiz.explain: Light comes back from droplets in front of you only if the Sun is behind you.
steps: A rainbow is always seen opposite to the Sun.
Light returns from droplets in front of you only if the Sun is behind you.
So look away from the Sun, with the Sun behind you.
Answer: Away from the Sun, with the Sun behind you
quiz.mistake: Assumes rainbows appear near the Sun

quiz.q: How many colours are usually listed in the spectrum of white light?
quiz.explain: VIBGYOR: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red — seven colours.
steps: The colours are VIBGYOR.
Violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red → count = 7.
So 7 colours.
Answer: 7
quiz.mistake: Forgets indigo

teach.ask: Gappu sees colours on the wall from a glass prism: 'Where did these colours come from? Is the glass painted?'
teach.praise: Chirp! White light holds seven colours, and the prism bends each by a different amount — that's dispersion!
teach.nudge: Good! Why do the colours separate — do they bend by the same amount?

revise.summary: A prism bends light towards its base and splits white light into seven colours (VIBGYOR), because each colour bends by a different amount. A rainbow forms when water droplets refract, disperse and internally reflect sunlight.

learn.hook: Why is the sky blue and not green or red? Tiny air molecules are throwing blue light all around you!
points: Scattering: when light hits tiny particles, they send it off in different directions. The colour of scattered light depends on the size of the particles.
Tyndall effect: the path of a light beam becomes visible when it passes through a colloid, e.g. sunlight entering a smoky room or streaming through a dense forest canopy.

Very fine particles (such as air molecules) scatter mainly blue light, which has a shorter wavelength; larger particles scatter longer wavelengths; large enough particles make the scattered light look white.
The sky looks blue because air molecules and fine particles scatter blue light much more strongly than red light; red light's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue light.

Without an atmosphere there would be no scattering, so the sky would look dark — as astronauts at very high altitudes see. Red is used for danger signals because it is scattered the least by fog or smoke, so it can be seen from far away.

example.q: Think it through: why are traffic stop lights and danger signals red?
steps: Smoke and fog particles scatter light.
Red light has the longest wavelength among visible colours and is scattered least.
So red light travels farthest through fog and smoke and is seen from a distance.
example.answer: Red is scattered the least, so it stays visible from far away even in fog or smoke.

learn.reallife: On a winter morning in Delhi, you can see bright beams of sunlight through the fog between trees — the Tyndall effect in action.

quiz.q: Why does the clear sky look blue?
options: Air molecules scatter blue light more than red light
Blue light is absorbed by air
The Sun gives out only blue light
quiz.explain: Molecules smaller than the wavelength of visible light scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) much more strongly.
steps: Air molecules are very fine particles.
Fine particles scatter blue light (short wavelength) much more strongly than red.
This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all over the sky.
So the sky looks blue because air molecules scatter blue light more than red.
Answer: Air molecules scatter blue light more than red light
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sky reflects the sea

quiz.q: Sunlight passing through gaps in a forest canopy shows visible beams. This is due to —
quiz.explain: Tiny water droplets and dust in the air scatter the light, making the beam's path visible.
steps: Tiny water droplets and dust in the forest air scatter the sunlight.
This makes the path of the beam visible.
Visible beams from scattering by particles = Tyndall effect.
Answer: Tyndall effect (scattering by particles)
quiz.mistake: Confuses scattering with dispersion

quiz.q: Why are danger signals red in colour?
options: Red is the brightest colour at night only
Red light is scattered the least by fog and smoke
quiz.explain: Being least scattered, red light reaches far through fog or smoke.
steps: Red light is scattered the least by fog and smoke.
So red light travels far and can be seen from a distance.
That is why danger signals are red.
Answer: Red light is scattered the least by fog and smoke
quiz.mistake: Thinks maximum scattering makes a signal more visible

quiz.q: What would the sky look like to an astronaut far above the atmosphere?
quiz.explain: With no air to scatter sunlight, the sky appears dark.
steps: The blue sky is caused by scattering in the atmosphere.
Far above the atmosphere there is no air to scatter sunlight.
So the sky looks dark.
Answer: Dark
quiz.mistake: Assumes the sky is blue everywhere

quiz.q: Very large particles in the air scatter light so that it appears —
quiz.explain: When particles are large enough, all colours are scattered about equally, so the light looks white.
steps: Very fine particles scatter mainly blue; larger ones scatter longer wavelengths.
Large enough particles scatter all colours about equally.
All colours together look white.
Answer: White
quiz.mistake: Thinks bigger particles always scatter blue

quiz.q: The wavelength of red light is about how many times that of blue light?
quiz.explain: Red light's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue light, so it is scattered much less.
steps: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.
From the lesson: red's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue.
So the answer is 1.8.
Answer: 1.8
quiz.mistake: Guesses a much larger difference

quiz.q: The colour of scattered light depends mainly on —
options: The size of the scattering particles
quiz.explain: Fine particles scatter blue; larger ones scatter longer wavelengths; very large ones scatter all colours.
steps: Fine particles scatter blue; larger particles scatter longer wavelengths; very large ones scatter all colours.
So the colour depends mainly on the size of the scattering particles.
Answer: The size of the scattering particles
quiz.mistake: Does not connect colour with particle size

quiz.q: Which is an example of the Tyndall effect?
options: A beam of light visible in a smoke-filled room
A pencil looking bent in water
An image in a plane mirror
quiz.explain: Smoke particles scatter light, making the beam's path visible.
steps: Tyndall effect: a light beam's path becomes visible when particles scatter it.
Smoke particles in a room scatter light, showing the beam.
A rainbow is dispersion; a bent pencil is refraction; a mirror image is reflection.
So the beam in a smoke-filled room is the Tyndall effect.
Answer: A beam of light visible in a smoke-filled room
quiz.mistake: Confuses Tyndall effect with dispersion or refraction

teach.ask: Gappu looks up: 'Why is the sky blue? And why do astronauts say space looks black?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Air molecules scatter blue light the most — and with no air in space, there's nothing to scatter, so it's dark!
teach.nudge: Close! What do the tiny particles in air do to sunlight?

revise.summary: Tiny particles scatter light, and the colour scattered depends on particle size. Air molecules scatter blue most, making the sky blue; large particles scatter all colours (white). The Tyndall effect makes light beams visible, and red danger signals are least scattered.
